title: What Comes After & What Comes Before: Class 1 Numbers Made Easy (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: What Comes After and Before: Class 1 Numbers + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach Class 1 kids what comes after, before and between numbers to 100 with a hundred chart, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable practice worksheets.
excerpt: Knowing what comes after 29, before 60 or between 7 and 9 looks trivial, but it is where real number sense begins. Here is how to teach it in fifteen minutes a day, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Class 1 child what comes after 29 and you will often get a confident ‘twenty-ten’ before the penny drops and they fix it to thirty. That little stumble is not a mistake to worry about — it is the exact spot where number sense is being built. Knowing what comes after, what comes before, and what sits between two numbers is one of the first real skills in the Class 1 maths syllabus, and it does far more heavy lifting than it looks.

In my experience teaching six-year-olds, parents treat this as trivial — of course 6 comes after 5 — and then wonder why their child freezes at 39, 40 or 99. The skill is not about reciting the number song. It is about pulling any number out of the middle of the sequence and instantly knowing its neighbours, both ways.

What ‘after’, ‘before’ and ‘between’ actually mean

Keep the language precise from day one, because loose wording is where the confusion starts.

  • After means the very next number — one more. After 6 is 7.
  • Before means the number just gone — one less. Before 6 is 5.
  • Between means the number that fits snugly in the gap. Between 6 and 8 is 7.

Notice that ‘after’ is the same as adding one and ‘before’ is the same as taking one away. Say that out loud with your child. The moment they connect ‘before’ to ‘one less’, subtraction stops being a separate scary thing later on.

Why this tiny skill builds real number sense

Two of the biggest ideas in early maths hide inside it. The first is counting on and counting back — the ability to start from any number and move a step in either direction without going back to one. A child who can answer ‘what comes after 47’ instantly is really doing 47 + 1 in their head, which is the seed of mental addition.

The second is the number line. When a child knows every number has a fixed neighbour on the left and on the right, they are picturing numbers as points in order, not as a random list to be memorised. That mental picture pays off for years — in place value, in comparing numbers, and eventually in measurement and negative numbers.

How to teach what comes after and before with a hundred chart

The single best tool for this is a hundred chart — the ten-by-ten grid of numbers from 1 to 100. You can print one or draw it once on chart paper. Here is the routine I would use.

Start with a number, point to its neighbours

Put your finger on any number, say 34. ‘What comes after?’ The child slides one square right to 35. ‘What comes before?’ One square left to 33. Do ten of these a day. The physical sliding matters — it turns an abstract question into a movement they can feel.

Then hide the chart

After a week, ask the same questions without the chart in front of them. If they hesitate, let them picture the grid. The goal is for the answer to come from the pattern in their head, not from counting up from one every single time.

Watch the tens jumps

The tricky spots are the ends of each row — what comes after 39, after 59, after 99. On a hundred chart these are where you drop down to the next row, and they are exactly where children stumble. Spend extra time on 29, 39, 49 and so on until the jump to the next ten is automatic.

The confusion that trips up every Class 1 child

Nearly every child mixes up ‘before’ and ‘after’ at some point, and it is usually a language problem, not a maths one. ‘Before’ can sound like it should be the bigger, later number to a small child — the way ‘before bedtime’ can feel like later in the evening.

The fix that works: anchor ‘before’ to ‘smaller, one less’ and ‘after’ to ‘bigger, one more’, and say both every time for a few weeks. Do not assume it has stuck after one good day. This particular mix-up comes back, so keep testing it in both directions.

A quick reference of examples

QuestionThinkAnswer
After 7One more8
Before 7One less6
Between 7 and 9The gap8
After 39Jump to the next ten40
Before 60One less, end of a row59
After 99One more, into hundreds100

A realistic fifteen-minute routine

You do not need worksheets every day, though written practice helps lock it in. A pattern that works for the Tier-2 city parents I have advised: five minutes of chart pointing, five minutes of quick-fire oral questions in the car or kitchen, and a few written questions two or three times a week. Mix after, before and between in the same session so the child has to listen to the question rather than answer on autopilot.

One honest caveat — resist jumping straight to numbers up to 100 in week one. Master neighbours up to 20 first, then 50, then 100. A child who is rock solid to 20 will generalise the pattern to bigger numbers far faster than one who was rushed.

Test what your child knows

Below is a free eight-question quiz on exactly this skill — after, before and between, including the tricky tens jumps. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: What Comes After, Before and Between Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on after, before and between numbers up to 100. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: After means one more, so after 7 comes 8.
Before means one less, so before 10 comes 9.
6 fits in the gap between 5 and 7.
39 is the end of a row on a hundred chart, so the next number jumps to the next ten: 40.
One more than 99 is 100, the first three-digit number.

questions.q: Riya is on square 59 of a hundred chart. Which number comes right after?
questions.explanation: 59 is the end of a row, so one more drops to the next ten: 60.

faq.q: What should a Class 1 child know about before and after numbers?
faq.a: By the end of Class 1 a child should give the number that comes after, before or between any number up to 100 without counting from one — including the tricky jumps like after 39 or after 99.

faq.q: Why does my child keep confusing before and after?
faq.a: It is usually a language issue, not a maths one — ‘before’ can sound like the later number to a small child. Anchor ‘before’ to ‘one less’ and ‘after’ to ‘one more’ and repeat both every time for a few weeks.

faq.q: Up to which number should we practise?
faq.a: Start with neighbours up to 20 until they are automatic, then extend to 50, then to 100. Rushing to 100 too early is the most common reason children stall at the tens jumps.

faq.q: Do I really need a hundred chart to teach this?
faq.a: It is not compulsory, but it is the fastest tool. Sliding a finger one square right for ‘after’ and one square left for ‘before’ makes the idea physical, and the grid shows exactly why 40 follows 39.
